title: Checkpoint: The Periodic Table
objective: After this level you can use the periodic table to predict how an element behaves.
summary: Metallic character grows toward the lower left and nonmetallic character toward the upper right, so an element's position predicts its behavior, as with rubidium. One map holds the whole chapter.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: predict an element you've never met.
cards.body: Mendeleev predicted germanium from a gap. Now you have the full map. By the end of this level, an element's address will tell you much of what it does.

cards.headline: Two fierce corners, one calm column
cards.body: Metallic character is strongest at the left of the table and grows as you go down a group, so the most metallic elements sit at the lower left. Nonmetallic character peaks at the upper right. That puts the fiercest reactors in opposite corners: cesium, which explodes in water, at the lower left, and fluorine, the most reactive element, at the upper right. Beside fluorine runs the calmest column of all, the noble gases.

cards.headline: Reading an address
cards.body: Try rubidium, in group 1 between potassium and cesium. Its column says soft, reactive metal; its place in the column says fiercer than potassium. That's exactly right: rubidium reacts violently with water. Or take tennessine, element 117, made only in labs. Its column files it with the halogens. That's Mendeleev's trick, played on a finished map.

cards.headline: The whole chapter on one map
cards.body: Elements are the substances chemistry can't split. Mendeleev lined them up and predicted the gaps; today atomic number sets the order. Metals fill the left, nonmetals the upper right. Group 1 fizzes, group 17 grabs, group 18 shrugs. The first three elements came from the Big Bang, others up to iron from stars, and heavier ones from exploding and colliding stars.

mascot.line: One map, 118 elements, and now you can read it. Chapter 3, done.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How an element's place on the periodic table predicts how it will behave.
How Mendeleev spotted a repeating pattern and used its gaps to predict missing elements.
Why full outer shells keep noble gases calm while one loose outer electron makes alkali metals wild.
Where the elements came from: the Big Bang, stars, exploding stars and labs.

questions.prompt: Periodic table recap: where are the most metallic elements found?

options.label: At the upper right
options.rationale: The upper right is where nonmetallic character peaks.

options.label: Along the top row
options.rationale: Metallic character grows as you go down, not up.

questions.explanation: Metallic character is strongest at the left and increases down a group.

questions.prompt: Periodic table recap: rubidium sits in group 1, just below potassium. What should you predict?

options.label: It reacts with water even more fiercely
It is an unreactive gas like neon
options.rationale: Group 1 holds reactive metals, not noble gases.

options.label: It is a brittle, dull nonmetal
options.rationale: The lower left is metal territory.

options.label: It reacts less than lithium does

questions.explanation: Group 1 reactivity rises down the column, and rubidium does react violently with water.

questions.prompt: Periodic table recap: what did Mendeleev do with the gaps in his table?

options.label: Filled them with guesses from alchemy
options.rationale: He predicted from the pattern, not from alchemy.

options.label: Removed them in later versions
options.rationale: He kept the gaps, and they were filled.

options.label: Put the noble gases there
options.rationale: The gaps were for elements like gallium and germanium.

options.label: Predicted the elements that would fill them

questions.explanation: He predicted properties for missing elements; gallium, scandium and germanium later fit.

questions.prompt: Periodic table recap: going down their columns, how do alkali metals and halogens change in reactivity?

options.label: Both get more reactive
options.rationale: Halogens get less reactive down the group.

options.label: Alkali metals get more reactive; halogens get less
Both get less reactive
options.rationale: Alkali metals get more reactive down the group.

options.label: Alkali metals get less reactive; halogens get more

questions.explanation: Cesium is fiercer than lithium, but fluorine is fiercer than iodine: the trends run opposite.

questions.prompt: Periodic table recap: where were natural elements heavier than iron made?

options.label: In the Big Bang
options.rationale: The Big Bang made only hydrogen, helium and some lithium.

options.label: By fusion inside ordinary stars
options.rationale: Fusion in stars stops at iron.

options.label: In supernovas and neutron star collisions
Only in laboratories
options.rationale: Labs made the transuranium elements, not gold or platinum.

questions.explanation: Supernovas and neutron star mergers supplied the energy that stars alone could not.
